To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the brain encodes word sequences in a hierarchical manner, with lower levels encoding phonemes and higher levels encoding syntactic and semantic information; and 2) decoding speech directly from neural signals using a hierarchical language model produces lower word error rates than previous decoding methods that use lower-level motor or auditory features.

the decoding of speech from neural signals can be improved by using word sequences instead of motor or auditory features, and that this improvement can be explained by the higher-level language goals of speech.

(1) decoding neural signals directly to words outperforms decoding to phonemes or syllables; (2) decoding to words improves as the number of words in the vocabulary increases, whereas decoding to phonemes and syllables do not; and (3) decoding to words can achieve a similar word error rate as decoding to phonemes, but at a lower bit rate, suggesting that decoding to words is an efficient way to achieve high performance in a speech decoding task.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a brain-computer-interface (BCI) for speech communication based on the decoding of speech motor commands directly from the human brain.
the development of speech decoding algorithms based on direct mapping of brain signals to speech sounds.
the development of novel methods for the decoding of speech from the brain activity of people with paralysis or severe speech impairment.
